newsitem.title: PERU: Peru Congress set to extend secret courts.
newsitem.headline: Peru Congress set to extend secret courts.

text.p: Peru's congressional Justice Committee has voted to extend for a year the controversial "faceless" courts that have jailed thousands of guerrillas but also put hundreds of innocent people behind bars.

"These courts will exist for as long as the phenomenon of terrorism exists in our country," Congress' Justice Commmitte President Oscar Medelios said on local radio, following the vote late on Monday.
The extension will not come into effect until a scheduled vote on Thursday in the single-chamber Congress, where, as on the Justice Committee, government parties have a comfortable majority.
Under current legislation the tribunals, whose anonymous judges often wear hoods or sit behind one-way screens, were due to end their functions on Oct. 15.
But a series of top government officials have publicly backed extending the secret court system, which President Alberto Fujimori introduced in 1992 to combat escalating guerrilla violence.
Fujimori brought in the system as part of a tough anti-guerrilla strategy, arguing normal courts were failing to convict terrorists through incompetence, corruption or fear.
But human rights groups at home and abroad have villified the system for jailing suspects on flimsy evidence, often obtained by torture, and without the chance of a fair trial.
The government, which has since 1995 released nearly 250 innocent prisoners falsely convicted of terrorism, admits up to 400 more wrongly accused inmates may still be behind bars.
Last week Peru's ombudsman, Jorge Santistevan, one of three members of a special commission created to recommend pardons for innocent prisoners, called for an end to the functions of the courts.
Although greatly weakened since the 1992 capture of its leader Abimael Guzman, Shining Path has increased activity with a series of car-bombs, assassinations and clashes.
